entries.ec94a21d85ca3203ebe8bfcfd0a9369408c4a89c: <div sID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="86" osisID="Ps.86" sID="Ps.86"/> <div eID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12024" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12025" type="x-p"/> This psalm is entitled "a prayer of David;" probably it was not penned upon any particular occasion, but was a prayer he often used himself, and recommended to others for their use, especially in a day of affliction. Many think that David penned this prayer as a type of Christ, "who in the days of his flesh offered up strong cries," <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. David, in this prayer (according to the nature of that duty), I. Gives glory to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.8-Ps.86.10">ver. 8-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.12">12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.13">13</reference>. II. Seeks for grace and favour from God, that God would hear his prayers ( <reference osisRef="Ps.86.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.7">7</reference>), preserve and save him, and be merciful to him ( <reference osisRef="Ps.86.2-Ps.86.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">16</reference>), that he would give him joy, and grace, and strength, and put honour upon him, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.17">17</reference>. He pleads God's goodness ( <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">15</reference>) and the malice of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">ver. 14</reference>. In singing this we must, as David did, lift up our souls to God with application.
entries.d2685ab2adadad2f504bee84f09615244fb8d7eb: <div eID="gen12025" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12024" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Humble Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen12026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Bow down thine ear, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , hear me: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> poor and needy. <hi type="super">2</hi> Preserve my soul; for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee. <hi type="super">3</hi> Be merciful unto me, O Lord: for I cry unto thee daily. <hi type="super">4</hi> Rejoice the soul of thy servant: for unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul. <hi type="super">5</hi> For thou, Lord, <hi type="italic">art</hi> good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> Give ear, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , unto my prayer; and attend to the voice of my supplications. <hi type="super">7</hi> In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me. <div eID="gen12026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12027" type="x-p"/> This psalm was published under the title of <hi type="italic">a prayer of David;</hi> not as if David sung all his prayers, but into some of his songs he inserted prayers; for a psalm will admit the expressions of any pious and devout affections. But it is observable how very plain the language of this psalm is, and how little there is in it of poetic flights or figures, in comparison with some other psalms; for the flourishes of wit are not the proper ornaments of prayer. Now here we may observe, <div eID="gen12027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12028" type="x-p"/> I. The petitions he puts up to God. It is true, prayer accidentally may preach, but it is most fit that (as it is in this prayer) every passage should be directed to God, for such is the nature of prayer as it is here described (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Unto thee, O Lord! do I lift up my soul,</hi> as he had said <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Ps. xxv. 1</reference>. In all the parts of prayer the soul must ascend upon the wings of faith and holy desire, and be lifted up to God, to meet the communications of his grace, and in an expectation raised very high of great things from him. 1. He begs that God would give a gracious audience to his prayers (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Bow down thy ear, O Lord! hear me.</hi> When God hears our prayers it is fitly said that he <hi type="italic">bows down his ear</hi> to them, for it is admirable condescension in God that he is pleased to take notice of such mean creatures as we are and such defective prayers as ours are. He repeats this again (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Give ear, O Lord! unto my prayer,</hi> a favourable ear, though it be whispered, though it be stammered; <hi type="italic">attend to the voice of my supplications.</hi>" Not that God needs to have his affection stirred up by any thing that we can say; but thus we must express our desire of his favour. The Son of David spoke it with assurance and pleasure (<reference osisRef="John.11.41-John.11.42">John xi. 41, 42</reference>), <hi type="italic">Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me; and I know that thou hearest me always.</hi> 2. He begs that God would take him under his special protection, and so be the author of his salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Preserve my soul; save thy servant.</hi> It was David's soul that was God's servant; for those only serve God acceptably that <hi type="italic">serve him with their spirits.</hi> David's concern is about his soul; if we understand it of his natural life, it teaches us that the best self-preservation is to commit ourselves to God's keeping and by faith and prayer to make our Creator our preserver. But it may be understood of his spiritual life, the life of the soul as distinct from the body: "Preserve my soul from that one evil and dangerous thing to souls, even from sin; preserve my soul, and so save me." All those whom God will save he preserves, and will preserve them to his heavenly kingdom. 3. He begs that God would look upon him with an eye of pity and compassion (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be merciful to me, O Lord!</hi> It is mercy in God to pardon our sins and to help us out of our distresses; both these are included in this prayer, <hi type="italic">God be merciful to me.</hi> "Men show no mercy; we ourselves deserve no mercy, but, Lord, for mercy-sake, be <hi type="italic">merciful unto me.</hi>" 4. He begs that God would fill him with inward comfort (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rejoice the soul of thy servant.</hi> It is God only that can <hi type="italic">put gladness into the heart and make the soul to rejoice,</hi> and then, and not till then, the joy is full; and, as it is the duty of those who are God's servants to <hi type="italic">serve him with gladness,</hi> so it is their privilege to be <hi type="italic">filled with joy and peace in believing,</hi> and they may in faith pray, not only that God will preserve their souls, but that he will rejoice their souls, and the <hi type="italic">joy of the Lord</hi> will be <hi type="italic">their strength.</hi> Observe, When he prays, <hi type="italic">Rejoice my soul,</hi> he adds, <hi type="italic">For unto thee do I lift up my soul.</hi> Then we may expect comfort from God when we take care to keep up our communion with God: prayer is the nurse of spiritual joy. <div eID="gen12028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12029" type="x-p"/> II. The pleas with which he enforces these petitions. 1. He pleads his relation to God and interest in him: "Thou art my God, to whom I have devoted myself, and on whom I depend, and I am thy servant (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">v. 2</reference>), in subjection to thee, and therefore looking for protection from thee." 2. He pleads his distress: "<hi type="italic">Hear me, for I am poor and needy,</hi> therefore I want thy help, therefore none else will hear me." God is the poor man's King, whose glory it is to <hi type="italic">save the souls of the needy;</hi> those who are poor in spirit, who see themselves empty and necessitous, are most welcome to the God of all grace. 3. He pleads God's good will towards all that seek him (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">v. 5</reference>): "To thee do I <hi type="italic">lift up my soul</hi> in desire and expectation; <hi type="italic">for thou, Lord, art good;</hi>" and whither should beggars go but to the door of the good house-keeper? The goodness of God's nature is a great encouragement to us in all our addresses to him. His goodness appears in two things, giving and forgiving. (1.) He is a sin-pardoning God; not only he can forgive, but he is ready to forgive, more ready to forgive than we are to repent. <hi type="italic">I said, I will confess, and thou forgavest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">Ps. xxxii. 5</reference>. (2.) He is a prayer-hearing God; he is plenteous in mercy, very full, and very free, both rich and liberal unto <hi type="italic">all those that call upon him;</hi> he has wherewithal to supply all their needs and is openhanded in granting that supply. 4. He pleads God's good work in himself, by which he had qualified him for the tokens of his favour. Three things were wrought in him by divine grace, which he looked upon as earnests of all good:—(1.) A conformity to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am holy,</hi> therefore preserve my soul; for those whom the Spirit sanctifies he will preserve. He does not say this in pride and vain glory, but with humble thankfulness to God. <hi type="italic">I am one whom thou favourest</hi> (so the margin reads it), whom thou hast <hi type="italic">set apart for thyself.</hi> If God has begun a good work of grace in us, we must own that <hi type="italic">the time was a time of love. Then was I in his eyes as one that found favour,</hi> and whom God hath taken into his favour he will take under his protection. <hi type="italic">All his saints are in thy hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">Deut. xxxiii. 3</reference>. Observe, <hi type="italic">I am needy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.1">v. 1</reference>), yet <hi type="italic">I am holy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">v. 2</reference>), holy and yet needy, <hi type="italic">poor in the world, but rich in faith.</hi> Those who preserve their purity in their greatest poverty may assure themselves that God will preserve their comforts, will preserve their souls. (2.) A confidence in God: <hi type="italic">Save thy servant that trusteth in thee.</hi> Those that are holy must nevertheless not trust in themselves, nor in their own righteousness, but only in God and his grace. Those that trust in God may expect salvation from him. (3.) A disposition to communion with God. He hopes God will answer his prayers, because he had inclined him to pray. [1.] To be constant in prayer: <hi type="italic">I cry unto thee daily, and all the day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.86.3">v. 3</reference>. It is thus our duty to pray always, without ceasing, and to continue instant in prayer; and then we may hope to have our prayers heard which we make in the time of trouble, if we have made conscience of the duty at other times, at all times. It is comfortable if an affliction finds the wheels of prayer a-going, and that they are not then to be set a-going. [2.] To be inward with God in prayer, to <hi type="italic">lift up his soul</hi> to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">v. 4</reference>. Then we may hope that God will meet us with his mercies, when we in our prayers send forth our souls as it were to meet him. [3.] To be in a special manner earnest with God in prayer when he was in affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In the day of my trouble,</hi> whatever others do, <hi type="italic">I will call upon thee,</hi> and commit my case to thee, for thou wilt hear and answer me, and I shall not seek in vain, as those did who cried, <hi type="italic">O Baal! hear us; but there was no voice, nor any that regarded,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.29">1 Kings xviii. 29</reference>.
entries.5c25cd38e9448b3a73686f725d7c1f0f8dced675: <div eID="gen12029" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Petitions and Praises; Prayer for Mercy and Grace.</title> <div sID="gen12030" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Among the gods <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like unto thee, O Lord; neither <hi type="italic">are there any works</hi> like unto thy works. <hi type="super">9</hi> All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name. <hi type="super">10</hi> For thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> great, and doest wondrous things: thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> God alone. <hi type="super">11</hi> Teach me thy way, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name. <hi type="super">12</hi> I will praise thee, O Lord my God, with all my heart: and I will glorify thy name for evermore. <hi type="super">13</hi> For great <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell. <hi type="super">14</hi> O God, the proud are risen against me, and the assemblies of violent <hi type="italic">men</hi> have sought after my soul; and have not set thee before them. <hi type="super">15</hi> But thou, O Lord, <hi type="italic">art</hi> a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth. <hi type="super">16</hi> O turn unto me, and have mercy upon me; give thy strength unto thy servant, and save the son of thine handmaid. <hi type="super">17</hi> show me a token for good; that they which hate me may see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and be ashamed: because thou, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , hast holpen me, and comforted me. <div eID="gen12030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12031" type="x-p"/> David is here going on in his prayer. <div eID="gen12031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12032" type="x-p"/> I. He gives glory to God; for we ought in our prayers to praise him, ascribing kingdom, power, and glory, to him, with the most humble and reverent adorations. 1. As a being of unparalleled perfection, such a one that there is none like him nor any to be compared with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.8">v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Among the gods,</hi> the false gods, whom the heathens worshipped, the angels, the kings of the earth, among them all, <hi type="italic">there is none like unto thee, O Lord!</hi> none so wise, so mighty, so good; <hi type="italic">neither are there any works like unto thy works,</hi> which is an undeniable proof that there is none like him; his own works praise him, and the best way we have of praising him is by acknowledging that there is none like him. 2. As the fountain of all being and the centre of all praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast made all nations,</hi> made them all of one blood; they all derive their being from thee, and have a constant dependence on thee, and therefore <hi type="italic">they shall come and worship before thee and glorify thy name.</hi>" This was in part fulfilled in the multitude of proselytes to the Jewish religion in the days of David and Solomon, but was to have its full accomplishment in the days of the Messiah, when some out of every kingdom and nation should be effectually brought in to praise God, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. It was by Christ that God made all nations, for without him was not any thing made that was made, and therefore through Christ, and by the power of his gospel and grace, all nations shall be brought to <hi type="italic">worship before God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Isa. lxvi. 23</reference>. 3. As a being infinitely great (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.10">v. 10</reference>): "Therefore all nations shall worship before thee, because as King of nations <hi type="italic">thou art great,</hi> thy sovereignty absolute and incontestable, thy majesty terrible and insupportable, thy power universal and irresistible, thy riches vast and inexhaustible, thy dominion boundless and unquestionable; and, for the proof of this, <hi type="italic">thou doest wondrous things,</hi> which all nations admire, and whence they might easily infer that thou art God alone, not only none like thee, but none besides thee." Let us always entertain great thoughts of this great God, and be filled with holy admiration of this God who doeth wonders; and let him alone have our hearts who is God alone. 4. As a being infinitely good. Man is bad, very wicked and vile (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">v. 14</reference>); no mercy is to be expected from him; <hi type="italic">but thou, O Lord! art a God full of compassion, and gracious,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">v. 15</reference>. This is that attribute by which he proclaims his name, and by which we are therefore to proclaim it, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7">Exod. xxxiv. 6, 7</reference>. It is his goodness that is over all his works, and therefore should fill all our praises; and this is our comfort, in reference to the wickedness of the world we live in, that, however it be, God is good. Men are barbarous, but God is gracious; men are false, but God is faithful. God is not only compassionate, but full of compassion, and in him <hi type="italic">mercy rejoiceth against judgment.</hi> He is long-suffering towards us, though we forfeit his favour and provoke him to anger, and he is <hi type="italic">plenteous in mercy and truth,</hi> as faithful in performing as he was free in promising. 5. As a kind friend and bountiful benefactor to him. We ought to praise God as good in himself, but we do it most feelingly when we observe how good he has been to us. This therefore the psalmist dwells upon with most pleasure, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.12-Ps.86.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. He had said (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">All nations shall praise thee, O Lord! and glorify thy name.</hi> It is some satisfaction to a good man to think that others shall praise and glorify God, but it is his greatest care and pleasure to do it himself. "Whatever others do" (says David), "<hi type="italic">I will praise thee, O Lord my God!</hi> not only as the Lord, but as my God; and I will do it with all my heart; I will be ready to do it and cordial in it; I will do it with cheerfulness and liveliness, with a sincere regard to thy honour; for <hi type="italic">I will glorify thy name,</hi> not for a time, but for evermore. I will do it as long as I live, and hope to be doing it to eternity." With good reason does he resolve to be thus particular in praising God, because God had shown him particular favours: <hi type="italic">For great is thy mercy towards me.</hi> The fountain of mercy is inexhaustibly full; the streams of mercy are inestimably rich. When we speak of God's mercy to us, it becomes us thus to magnify it: <hi type="italic">Great is thy mercy towards me.</hi> Of the greatness of God's mercy he gives this instance, <hi type="italic">Thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell,</hi> from death, from so great a death, as St. Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.10">2 Cor. i. 10</reference>), from eternal death, so even some of the Jewish writers understand it. David knew he deserved to be cast off for ever into the lowest hell for his sin in the matter of Uriah; but Nathan assured him that the Lord had <hi type="italic">taken away his sin,</hi> and by that word he was delivered from the lowest hell, and herein God's mercy was great towards him. Even the best saints owe it, not to their own merit, but to the mercy of God, that they are saved from the lowest hell; and the consideration of that should greatly enlarge their hearts in praising the mercy of God, which they are obliged to glorify for evermore. So glorious; so gracious, a rescue from everlasting misery, justly requires the return of everlasting praise. <div eID="gen12032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12033" type="x-p"/> II. He prays earnestly for mercy and grace from God. He complains of the restless and implacable malice of his enemies against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">v. 14</reference>): "Lord, be thou for me; for there are many against me." He then takes notice of their character; they were <hi type="italic">proud men</hi> that looked with disdain upon poor David. (Many are made persecutors by their pride.) They were <hi type="italic">violent men,</hi> that would carry all before them by force, right or wrong. They were <hi type="italic">terrible formidable men</hi> (so some), that did what they could to frighten all about them. He notices their number: There were <hi type="italic">assemblies</hi> of them; they were men in authority and met in councils and courts, or men for conversation, and met in clubs; but, being assembled, they were the more capable of doing mischief. He notices their enmity to him: "They <hi type="italic">rise up against me</hi> in open rebellion; they not only plot, but they put their plots in execution as far as they can; and the design is not only to depose me, but to destroy me: they seek after my life, to slay me; after my soul, to damn me, if it lay in their power." And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> He notices their distance and estrangement from God, which were at the bottom of their enmity to David: "<hi type="italic">They have not set thee before them;</hi> and what good can be expected from those that have no fear of God before their eyes? Lord, appear against them, for they are thy enemies as well as mine." His petitions are, <div eID="gen12033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12034" type="x-p"/> 1. For the operations of God's grace in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">v. 11</reference>. He prays that God would give him, (1.) An understanding heart, that he would inform and instruct him concerning his duty: "<hi type="italic">Teach me thy way, O Lord!</hi> the way that thou hast appointed me to walk in; when I am in doubt concerning it, make it plain to me what I should do; let me hear the voice saying, <hi type="italic">This is the way,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.30.21">Isa. xxx. 21</reference>. David was well taught in the things of God, and yet was sensible he needed further instruction, and many a time could not trust his own judgment: <hi type="italic">Teach me thy way; I will walk in thy truth.</hi> One would think it should be, <hi type="italic">Teach me thy truth, and I will walk in thy way;</hi> but it comes all to one; it is the way of truth that God teaches and that we must choose to walk in, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.30">Ps. cxix. 30</reference>. Christ is the way and the truth, and we must both learn Christ and walk in him. We cannot walk in God's way and truth unless he teach us; and, if we expect he should teach us, we must resolve to be governed by his teachings, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>. (2.) An upright heart: "<hi type="italic">Unite my heart to fear thy name.</hi> Make me sincere in religion. A hypocrite has a double heart; let mine be single and entire for God, not divided between him and the world, not straggling from him." Our hearts are apt to wander and hang loose; their powers and faculties wander after a thousand foreign things; we have therefore need of God's grace to unite them, that we may serve God with all that is within us, and all little enough to be employed in his service. "Let my heart be fixed for God, and firm and faithful to him, and fervent in serving him; that is a united heart." <div eID="gen12034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12035" type="x-p"/> 2. For the tokens of God's favour to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16-Ps.86.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Three things he here prays for:—(1.) That God would speak peace and comfort to him: "<hi type="italic">O turn unto me,</hi> as to one thou lovest and hast a kind and tender concern for. My enemies turn against me, my friends turn from me; Lord, do thou turn to me and have mercy upon me; it will be a comfort to me to know that thou pitiest me." (2.) That God would work deliverance for him, and set him in safety: "Give me <hi type="italic">thy strength;</hi> put strength into me, that I may help myself, and put forth thy strength for me, that I may be saved out of the hands of those that seek my ruin." He pleads relation: "I am <hi type="italic">thy servant;</hi> I am so by birth, as <hi type="italic">the son of thy handmaid,</hi> born in thy house, and therefore thou art my rightful owner and proprietor, from whom I may expect protection. <hi type="italic">I am thine; save me.</hi>" The children of godly parents, who were betimes dedicated to the Lord, may plead it with him; if they come under the discipline of his family, they are entitled to the privileges of it. (3.) That God would put a reputation on him: "<hi type="italic">Show me a token for good;</hi> make it to appear to others as well as to myself that thou art doing me good, and designing further good for me. Let me have some unquestionable illustrious instances of thy favour to me, <hi type="italic">that those who hate me may see it, and be ashamed</hi> of their enmity to me, as they will have reason to be when they perceive that <hi type="italic">thou, Lord, hast helped me and comforted me,</hi> and that therefore they have been striving against God, opposing one whom he owns, and that they have been striving in vain to ruin and vex one whom God himself has undertaken to help and comfort." The joy of the saints shall be the shame of their persecutors.  <chapter eID="Ps.86"/> <div eID="gen12035" type="x-p"/>

entries.6b8ca8274c6a46a70fb30ea1714de388370d32c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6494"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 86</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.1-Ps.86.17">Psa 86:1-17</reference>. This is a prayer in which the writer, with deep emotion, mingles petitions and praises, now urgent for help, and now elated with hope, in view of former mercies. The occurrence of many terms and phrases peculiar to David's Psalms clearly intimates its authorship.</title> <div sID="gen9951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6494"/><hi type="bold">1-2. poor and needy--</hi>a suffering child of God, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.12">Psa 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.27">18:27</reference>.<div eID="gen9951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am holy--</hi>or, "godly," as in <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">85:8</reference>. <div eID="gen9952" type="x-p"/>

entries.65a032b601effe63817508f83e605651a8dbe826: <div eID="gen21387" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21388" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21389" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21389" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21388" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21390" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays to God for support, from a conviction that he is merciful, good, ready to forgive, and that there is none like him, <reference osisRef="Psa.86.1-Psa.86.8">Psa 86:1-8</reference>; all nations shall bow before him because of his wondrous works, <reference osisRef="Psa.86.9">Psa 86:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.86.10">Psa 86:10</reference>; he prays to be instructed, and promises to praise God for his great mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.86.11-Psa.86.13">Psa 86:11-13</reference>; describes his enemies, and appeals to God, <reference osisRef="Psa.86.14-Psa.86.16">Psa 86:14-16</reference>; begs a token for God, that his enemies may be confounded, <reference osisRef="Psa.86.17">Psa 86:17</reference>. <div eID="gen21390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21391" type="x-p"/> The title attributes this Psalm to David; and in this all the versions agree: but in its structure it is the same with those attributed to the sons of Korah; and was probably made during the captivity. It is a very suitable prayer for a person laboring under affliction from persecution or calumny. <div eID="gen21391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21392" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21393" type="x-p"/> Bow down thine ear - Spoken after the manner of men: I am so low, and so weak, that, unless thou stoop to me, my voice cannot reach thee. <div eID="gen21393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21394" type="x-p"/> Poor and needy - I am afflicted, and destitute of the necessaries of life.
entries.b3860227de71c7e9f96216d275850af9d17a7e02: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21395" type="x-p"/> Preserve my soul - Keep it as in a strong place. <div eID="gen21395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21396" type="x-p"/> For I am holy - כי חשיד אני ki chasid ani, for I am merciful. The spirit of this prayer is, "The mercy I to others show, <div eID="gen21396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21397" type="x-p"/> That mercy show to me!" <div eID="gen21397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21398" type="x-p"/> Save thy servant - I have long taken thee as my Master and Lord; I receive the word from thy mouth, and obey thee.
entries.3c0c9cddbeff81f908f22ecb1634e36598bba4d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21399" type="x-p"/> Be merciful unto me - I have no merit; I plead none, but trust in thee alone. <div eID="gen21399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21400" type="x-p"/> I cry unto thee daily - My state deeply affects me; and I incessantly cry for thy salvation.
entries.efb7c83bcb9e27f05af02561b3cf31eb6e603805: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21401" type="x-p"/> Rejoice the soul of thy servant - I want spiritual blessings; I want such consolations as thou dost impart to them that love thee; I present that soul to thee which I wish thee to console.
entries.aeb019366df6c8c4276796fd38e83c1238c8d9fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21402" type="x-p"/> For thou, Lord, art good - I found my expectations of help on thy own goodness through which thou art always ready to forgive. And I found it also on thy well-known character, to which all thy followers bear testimony, viz., that "thou art plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee."
entries.e0191cae3d7a6b33ae1b706b1bad2380b2e74ee3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21403" type="x-p"/> Give ear, O Lord - Attend to me. Millions call upon thee for help and mercy; but who has more need than myself? That the psalmist was deeply in earnest, his conduct shows. <div eID="gen21403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21404" type="x-p"/> 1. He prayed. <div eID="gen21404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21405" type="x-p"/> 2. His prayer was vehement; he lifted up his voice. <div eID="gen21405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21406" type="x-p"/> 3. He continued in prayer; he abounded in supplications.
entries.0e7765d7f2f4d373dabda128283d88d9286edba6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21407" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt answer me - Because thou art good, merciful, and ready to forgive; and I call upon thee fervently, and seek thee in thy own way.
entries.2844a8cc36087b9edbd30b4d6863c6b8f9798d69: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21408" type="x-p"/> Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord - None that trusted in an idol ever had help in time of need; none that prayed to any of them ever had an answer to his petitions. Thou savest; they cannot; thou upholdest; they must be upheld by their foolish worshippers. Thou art my Director, אדני Adonai; but they cannot direct nor teach; they have mouths, but they speak not.
entries.d0b472041025808514a4ca2aca4cb44fb95a60c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21409" type="x-p"/> All nations - Thy word shall be proclaimed among all the Gentiles: they shall receive thy testimony, and worship thee as the only true and living God.
entries.4e663738a5278a43dcbe921376c218c151d51a97: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21410" type="x-p"/> For thou art great - Almighty, infinite, eternal. <div eID="gen21410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21411" type="x-p"/> And doest wondrous things - ועשה נפלאות veoseh niphlaoth; thou art the Worker of miracres. This thou hast done in numerous instances, and thereby showed thy infinite power and wisdom. <div eID="gen21411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21412" type="x-p"/> This appears to be a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ, and the evidence to be given to his Divine mission by the miracles which he should work. <div eID="gen21412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21413" type="x-p"/> Thou art God alone - Συ ει ὁ Θεος μονος ὁ μεγας - Sept. Thou art the only, The Great God. In this the Ethiopic and Arabic agree.
entries.ddc9c41523accba630cf184ceb3af798494da317: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21414" type="x-p"/> Teach me thy way - Instruct me in the steps I should take; for without thy teaching I must go astray. <div eID="gen21414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21415" type="x-p"/> Unite my heart - יחד לבבי yached lebabi, join all the purposes, resolutions, and affections of my heart together, to fear and to glorify thy name. This is a most important prayer. A divided heart is a great curse; scattered affections are a miserable plague. When the heart is not at unity with itself, the work of religion cannot go on. Indecision of mind and division of affections mar any work. The heart must be one, that the work may be one. If this be wanting, all is wrong. This is a prayer which becomes the mouth of every Christian.
entries.ff95f0bb6d246c66b938742bf0d006141153c3bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21416" type="x-p"/> I will praise thee - with all my heart - When my heart is united to fear thy name, then shall I praise thee with my whole heart.
entries.ed289578ce2525c8e56ac90ab5da4ff75e1ee06f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21417" type="x-p"/> Thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell - This must mean more than the grave; a hell below hell - a place of perdition for the soul, as the grave is a place of corruption for the body.
entries.089465eb16662a7f640b8911b7e4181bef65127e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21418" type="x-p"/> The assemblies of violent men - עדת עריצים adath aritsim, the congregation of the terrible ones. Men of violent passions, violent counsels, and violent acts; and, because they have power, terrible to all. <div eID="gen21418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21419" type="x-p"/> Have not set thee before them - Who sins that sets God before his eyes? Who does not sin that has no consciousness of the Divine presence?
entries.0c1c43dcaa55c439d68fbbdecd44f9d066d7a80c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21420" type="x-p"/> But thou, O Lord - What a wonderful character of God is given in this verse! אדני Adonai, the Director, Judge, and Support; - but instead of אדני Adonai, thirty-four of Kennicott's MSS. have יהוה Jehovah, the self-existent and eternal Being; - אל El, the strong God; רחום rachum, tenderly compassionate; חנון channun, the Dispenser of grace or favor; ארך אפים erech appayim, suffering long, not easily provoked; רב חמד rab chesed, abundant in blessings; and אמת emeth, faithful and true. Such is the God who has made himself more particularly known to us in Christ. The scanty language of our ancestors was not adequate to a full rendering of the original words: "And thu driht God gemildsiend, and mildheort, gethyldig and mucel mildheortnysse and sothfaest - And thou, Lord God, art mild, and mildhearted, patient, and of much mildheartedness, and soothfast," - steady in truth. <div eID="gen21420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21421" type="x-p"/> In the old Psalter the language is but little improved: And thou Lorde God mercier, and mercyful, sufferand, and of mykel mercy, and sothefast. <div eID="gen21421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21422" type="x-p"/> The word mercier is interpreted, do and dede of mercy.
entries.9e2ec10988b8d34ef24824b4126d4ba753901cd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21423" type="x-p"/> O turn unto me - He represents himself as following after God; but he cannot overtake him; and then he plays that he would turn and meet him through pity; or give him strength that he might be able to hold on his race. <div eID="gen21423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21424" type="x-p"/> Give thy strength unto thy servant - The Vulgate renders, Daniel imperium tuum puero tuo, "Give thy empire to thy child." The old Psalter. Gyf empyre to thi barne, and make safe the son of thi hand mayden. Thi barne - thy tender child. Anglo-Saxon; thy knave; signifying either a serving man or a male child. As many servants were found to be purloiners of their masters' property, hence the word knave, became the title of an unprincipled servant. The term fur, which signifies a thief in Latin, for the same reason became the appellative of a dishonest servant. <div eID="gen21424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21425" type="x-p"/> Quid domini facient, audent cum talia Fures? <div eID="gen21425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21426" type="x-p"/> When servants (thieves) do such things, what may not be expected from the masters? <div eID="gen21426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21427" type="x-p"/> Virg. Ecl. 3:16. <div eID="gen21427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21428" type="x-p"/> So Plautus, speaking of a servant, Aulul. 2:46, says: Homo es trium literarum, "Thou art a man of three letters," i.e., Fur, a thief. The word knave is still in use, but is always taken in a bad sense. The paraphrase in the old Psalter states the handmaid to be the kirk, and the son of this handmaid to be a true believer.
entries.eb49e21f3f371fcde1eb81e2dbd6af4f6455bf2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21429" type="x-p"/> Show me a token for good - עשה עמי אוה aseh immi oth "Make with me a sign." Fix the honourabie mark of thy name upon me, that I may be known to be thy servant. There seems to be an allusion here to the marking of a slave, to ascertain whose property he was. The Anglo-Saxon, "do with me a token in good.' Old Psalter: Do with me signe in gude. From tacn we have our word token, which signifies a sign, mark, or remembrancer of something beyond itself; a pledge that something, then specified, shall be done or given. Give me, from the influence of thy Spirit in my heart, a pledge that the blessings which I now ask shall be given in due time. But he wished for such a sign as his enemies might see; that they might know God to be his helper, and be confounded when they sought his destruction.  <chapter eID="Ps.86"/> <div eID="gen21429" type="x-p"/>

entries.f5886e6c8c1d7acfcc8632f23bc4a1b6ec73af4e: <div eID="gen9861" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer of a Persecuted Saint</title> <div sID="gen9862" type="x-p"/> A Psalm “by David” which has points of contact with <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.13">Psa 85:1-13</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">Psa 86:2</reference>, חסיד, with <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9">Psa 85:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">Psa 86:15</reference>, חסד ואמת, with <reference osisRef="Ps.85.11">Psa 85:11</reference>) is here inserted between Korahitic Psalms: it can only be called a Psalm by David as having grown out of Davidic and other model passages. The writer cannot be compared for poetical capability either with David or with the authors of such Psalms as Ps 116 and <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1">Psa 130:1</reference>-8. His Psalm is more liturgic than purely poetic, and it is also only entitled תּפּלּה, without bearing in itself any sign of musical designation. It possesses this characteristic, that the divine name אדני occurs seven times,<note placement="foot">For the genuine reading in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">Psa 86:4</reference> (where Heidenheim reads יהוה) and in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">Psa 86:5</reference> (where Nissel reads יהוה) is also אדני (Bomberg, Hutter, etc.). Both the divine names in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">Psa 86:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">Psa 86:5</reference> belong to the 134 ודּאין. The divine name אדני, which is written and is not merely substituted for יהוה, is called in the language of the Masora ודאי (the true and real one).</note> just as it occurs three times in <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference>, forming the start for a later, Adonajic style in imitation of the Elohimic.
entries.eb8d3a907e37100936cef74ff1e0b93c33226378: <reference osisRef="Ps.86.1-Ps.86.5">Psa 86:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen9862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9863" type="x-p"/> The prayer to be heard runs like <reference osisRef="Ps.55.3">Psa 55:3</reference>; and the statement of the ground on which it is based, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.1">Psa 86:1</reference></hi>, word for word like Ps 40:18. It is then particularly expressed as a prayer for preservation (שׁמרה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.167">Psa 119:167</reference>, although imperative, to be read <hi type="italic">shāmerah</hi>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.30.4">Psa 30:4</reference> מיּרדי, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.21">Psa 38:21</reference> רדפי or רדפי, and what we have already observed on <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference> שׁמרני); for he is not only in need of God’s help, but also because חסיד (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference>), i.e., united to Him in the bond of affection (חסד, Hos 6:4; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer 2:2</reference>), not unworthy of it. In <reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">Psa 86:2</reference> we hear the strains of <reference osisRef="Ps.25.20">Psa 25:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.7">Psa 31:7</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.3">Psa 86:3</reference>, of Psa 57:2.: the confirmation in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">Psa 86:4</reference></hi> is taken verbally from <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>, cf. also Psa 130:6. Here, what is said in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">Psa 86:4</reference> of this shorter Adonajic Psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference>, is abbreviated in the ἅπαξ γεγραμ. סלּח (root סל, של, to allow to hang loose, χαλᾶν, to give up, <hi type="italic">remittere</hi>). The Lord is good (טּוב), i.e., altogether love, and for this very reason also ready to forgive, and great and rich in mercy for all who call upon Him as such. The beginning of the following group also accords with <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference> in Psa 86:2.
entries.a238298c8333548835c111c4e6ec6ec0ed721e03: <reference osisRef="Ps.86.6-Ps.86.13">Psa 86:6-13</reference> <div eID="gen9863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9864" type="x-p"/> Here, too, almost everything is an echo of earlier language of the Psalms and of the Law; viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.86.7">Psa 86:7</reference> follows <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">Psa 17:6</reference> and other passages; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.8">Psa 86:8</reference> </hi>is taken from <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.9">Psa 89:9</reference>, where, however, אלהים, gods, is avoided; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.8">Psa 86:8</reference></hi> follows <reference osisRef="Deut.3.24">Deu 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.9">Psa 86:9</reference> follows <reference osisRef="Ps.22.28">Psa 22:28</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Psa 86:11</reference></hi> is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Psa 86:11</reference></hi> from <reference osisRef="Ps.26.3">Psa 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.13">Psa 86:13</reference>, שׁאול תּחתּיּה from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.22">Deu 32:22</reference>, where instead of this it is תּחתּית, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Psa 130:2</reference> תּחנוּני (supplicatory prayer) instead of תּחנוּנותי (importunate supplications); and also <reference osisRef="Ps.86.10">Psa 86:10</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.72.18">Psa 72:18</reference>) is a doxological formula that was already in existence. The construction הקשׁיב בּ is the same as in Psa 66:19. But although for the most part flowing on only in the language of prayer borrowed from earlier periods, this Psalm is, moreover, not without remarkable significance and beauty. With the confession of the incomparableness of the Lord is combined the prospect of the recognition of the incomparable One throughout the nations of the earth. This clear unallegorical prediction of the conversion of the heathen is the principal parallel to Rev 15:4. “All nations, which Thou hast made” - they have their being from Thee; and although they have forgotten it (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.9.18">Psa 9:18</reference>), they will nevertheless at last come to recognise it. כּל־גּוים, since the article is wanting, are nations of all tribes (countries and nationalities); cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16">Jer 16:16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">Psa 22:18</reference>; Tobit 13:11, ἔθνη πολλά, with <hi type="italic">ibid</hi>. <reference osisRef="Ps.14.6">Psa 14:6</reference>, πάντα τὰ ἔθνη. And how weightily brief and charming is the petition in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Psa 86:11</reference> : <hi type="italic">uni cor meum, ut timeat nomen tuum!</hi> Luther has rightly departed from the renderings of the lxx, Syriac, and Vulgate: <hi type="italic">laetetur</hi> (יחדּ from חדה). The meaning, however, is not so much “keep my heart near to the only thing,” as “direct all its powers and concentrate them on the one thing.” The following group shows us what is the meaning of the deliverance out of the hell beneath (שׁאול תּחתּיּה, like ארץ תּחתּית, the earth beneath, the inner parts of the earth, Eze 31:14.), for which the poet promises beforehand to manifest his thankfulness (כּי, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.13">Psa 86:13</reference>, as in Ps 56:14).
entries.5bb8e151b57acf9306bf7ea5a1fc53d37d0d9ca8: <reference osisRef="Ps.86.14-Ps.86.17">Psa 86:14-17</reference> <div eID="gen9864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9865" type="x-p"/> The situation is like that in the Psalms of the time of Saul. The writer is a persecuted one, and in constant peril of his life. He has taken <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">Psa 86:14</reference></hi> out of the Elohimic <reference osisRef="Ps.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference>, and retained the <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> as a proper name of God (cf. on the other hand <reference osisRef="Ps.86.8">Psa 86:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.10">Psa 86:10</reference>); he has, however, altered זרים to זרים, which here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference> (cf. however, <hi type="italic">ibid</hi>. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>), is the alternating word to עריצים. In <reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">Psa 86:15</reference> he supports his petition that follows by Jahve’s testimony concerning Himself in Exo 34:6. The appellation given to himself by the poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">Psa 86:16</reference> recurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference> (cf. Wisd. 9:5). The poet calls himself “the son of Thy handmaid” as having been born into the relation to Him of servant; it is a relationship that has come to him by birth. How beautifully does the <hi type="italic">Adonaj</hi> come in here for the seventh time! He is even from his mother’s womb the servant of the sovereign Lord, from whose omnipotence he can therefore also look for a miraculous interposition on his behalf. A “token for good” is a special dispensation, from which it becomes evident to him that God is kindly disposed towards him. לטובה as in the mouth of Nehemiah, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.19">Neh 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.31">Neh 13:31</reference>; of Ezr 8:22; and also even in Jeremiah and earlier. ויבשׁוּ is just as parenthetical as in Isa 26:11.  <chapter eID="Ps.86"/> <div eID="gen9865" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 86
In this psalm prayers and holy meditations, engaged in with the view of nourishing and confirming faith, together with praises and thanksgivings, are intermingled. It having been difficult in the judgement of carnal reason for David to escape from the distresses with which he was environed, he sets in opposition to its conclusions the infinite goodness and power of God. Nor does he simply request deliverance from his enemies; but he also prays that the fear of God may be implanted and firmly established in heart.
A Prayer of David.
Psalm 86:1-7
1. Incline thy ear, O Jehovah! answer me; for I am poor and needy. 2. Preserve my soul, for I am meek:
“Hezekiah, in the season of distress, 2 Kings 19:16, begins his prayer with these words: which may have occasioned the tradition of the Jews that he made use of this psalm on that occasion.” — Warner.
O my God! save thy servant who trusteth in thee. 3. Have mercy upon me, O Jehovah! for daily
In our English version it is, “for I am holy.” Cresswell would rather render, “for I am merciful and pious.” “That,” says he, “is the meaning of the Hebrew word, which the Septuagint and Jerome have rendered by holy. The Psalmist supplicates God’s favor upon five several grounds, namely, his destitution, (verse 1;) his mercifulness and goodness, (verse 2;) his trust in God, (verse 2;) his prayerfulness, (verses 3, 4;) and God’s goodness, (verse 5.”) — Cresswell.
do I cry to thee. 4. Make glad the soul of thy servant; for to thee, O Lord!
“Ou, tout le jour.” — Fr. marg. “Or, all the day.”
do I lift up my soul. 5. For thou, O Lord! art good, and gracious, and of great mercy to all who call upon thee. 6. Listen, O Jehovah! to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplications. 7. In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me.
 
1. Incline thy ear, O Jehovah! Neither the inscription nor the contents of this psalm enable us to conclude with certainty what dangers David here complains of; but the psalm in all probability refers to that period of his life when he was persecuted by Saul, and describes the train of thought which then occupied his mind, although it may not have been written until after his restoration to a state of outward peace and tranquillity, when he enjoyed greater leisure. He does not without cause allege before God the oppressions which he endured as a plea for obtaining the divine favor; for nothing is more suitable to the nature of God than to succor the afflicted: and the more severely any one is oppressed, and the more destitute he is of the resources of human aid, the more inclined is God graciously to help him. That despair therefore may not overwhelm our minds under our greatest afflictions, let us support ourselves from the consideration that the Holy Spirit has dictated this prayer for the poor and the afflicted.
